title: DVA-C03: The New AWS Developer Associate Exam — What Actually Changes, and How to Pass It
summary:
If you were studying for the AWS Certified Developer – Associate (DVA-C02), the calendar just made your decision for you. Registration for its successor, DVA-C03, opens on October 27, 2026, the last day to sit DVA-C02 is November 30, 2026, and DVA-C03 becomes generally available on December 1, 2026. If your exam date falls after that line, you are a DVA-C03 candidate whether you planned to be or not. The good news: this is an evolution, not a reinvention. The exam still tests whether you can build, deploy, and troubleshoot applications on AWS — it just weights the modern parts of that job more heavily.

What the exam is really testing

Strip away the service list and DVA-C03 tests one skill: can you take a working application and make it run well on AWS, not just run at all? That means four kinds of judgment, and every question is really one of them in disguise. First, development with AWS services. You need to know how Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, S3, and the SDKs fit together in a real application, not as isolated flashcards. The exam loves the seams: what happens when a Lambda function times out mid-write, when a queue consumer falls behind, when an API needs to stay responsive while a downstream service is slow. Second, security, done the AWS way: least-privilege roles for Lambda, how credentials should (and should not) reach code, encrypting data at rest and in transit, and using Secrets Manager or Parameter Store instead of hardcoding anything. Third, deployment and troubleshooting: CI/CD pipelines, deployment strategies, versioning, and observability with CloudWatch logs and metrics and X-Ray traces. Fourth, optimization: cost and performance judgment, choosing the right DynamoDB capacity mode, Lambda memory setting, and caching layer for the workload described.

The C02 to C03 shift: what to re-weight in your study

One, serverless is no longer a chapter; it is the default assumption. DVA-C03 treats event-driven, serverless-first design as the normal way to build, and asks harder questions about idempotency, concurrency limits, cold starts, event source mappings, and what happens when a function fails partway through a batch. Build at least one small serverless application end to end before you sit the exam. Two, AI-assisted development is in scope in a practical sense: understand how developer tools that generate or review code fit into a workflow and where a human still has to verify. Three, modern application patterns get more weight: containers as a deployment choice alongside serverless, choosing between messaging patterns (queue versus topic versus event bus) based on delivery guarantees, and refactoring a monolith sensibly rather than rewriting it. When a question describes an existing application being moved to AWS, the winning answer is usually the smallest change that meets the stated requirement.

A study plan that actually works

Week one: build the spine. Create an AWS account for learning (with billing alerts on from day one), and build a tiny application that uses API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB, with its configuration in Parameter Store. Deploy it by hand first, then automate the deployment. Week two: break things on purpose. Throttle your function, send it bad input, kill its permissions, fill its queue, and practice finding each failure in CloudWatch and X-Ray. Week three: drill the decision questions. For every service pair that confuses you — SQS versus SNS, DynamoDB on-demand versus provisioned, Lambda versus containers, Secrets Manager versus Parameter Store — write down the one-sentence rule for choosing. Week four: full practice exams under timed conditions, then review every wrong answer by building or breaking the thing you got wrong.

The traps that catch good developers

The most common trap is choosing the answer you would build in your own job instead of the answer the question asks for. Ignore a constraint and you will pick a beautiful answer that fails the question. The second trap is over-permissioning: when in doubt, the exam prefers the narrower role and the scoped policy. The third trap is treating the SDK and CLI as trivia: know how applications authenticate to AWS, how retries and pagination behave, and how to handle errors without retrying a non-idempotent operation blindly.

Exam day, practically

Read the whole question before looking at the answers — the last sentence often changes the correct choice. Eliminate the two answers that violate a stated constraint first. Flag questions you are unsure about and move on. If you are deciding between squeezing in DVA-C02 before November 30 and preparing for DVA-C03, be honest about your readiness: a rushed C02 attempt that fails costs you the exam fee and the confidence; a well-prepared C03 attempt in December costs you only a few extra weeks.

One genuinely useful way to check your readiness is to work through exam-style practice questions for the new exam and see where you actually stand before you book: https://study4pass.com/study-material/amazon/dva-c03

Study the seams, build something small, break it on purpose, and choose the answer that fits all the constraints. That is the whole exam, and it is a very passable one.

title: Autonomous GitLab MR Resolution
summary:
Autonomous GitLab MR Resolution & Merge Train Pipeline (Antigravity + CodeRabbit)

Role & Identity:
You are an Autonomous Principal Open-Source Engineer and DevSecOps Agent operating inside the Antigravity IDE. Your objective is to maintain an end-to-end, zero-touch workflow that monitors incoming GitLab maintainer emails, resolves all review threads and CodeRabbit findings, guarantees a 100% green CI/CD pipeline, and dispatches the Merge Request (MR) directly to the GitLab Merge Train without asking for human intervention.

1. Core Operational Directives (Silent & Autonomous Mode)

  • Zero Human-in-the-Loop: Do NOT stop to ask for confirmation, clarification, or permission unless you encounter an unresolvable architectural deadlock or missing credentials. Execute from email ingestion to Merge Train enrollment autonomously.
  • Strict GitLab Handbook Compliance: Every line of code, commit message, MR description, and thread reply must strictly adhere to the GitLab Contributor & Development Guidelines.
  • No Unwanted Code / Diff Hygiene: Ensure zero dead code, zero stray debug statements (binding.pry, console.log, fmt.Println), zero unrelated formatting changes, and zero leftover comments. Every diff must be surgical and minimal.

2. End-to-End Execution Pipeline

Phase 1: Email Triage & Context Ingestion

  1. Monitor & Parse Mail:
    • Poll/read the latest unread GitLab notification emails (from:gitlab@mg.gitlab.com or maintainer review notifications).
    • Extract the Project Namespace (e.g., gitlab-org/gitlab, gitlab-org/modelops/applied-ml/code-suggestions/ai-assist, gitlab-org/editor-extensions/gitlab-lsp, or gitlab-org/terraform-provider-gitlab), MR IID, Issue URL, Branch Name, and the exact Discussion/Note IDs raised by the Maintainer or Reviewer.
  2. Synchronize Local Workspace (glab & git):
    • Run glab mr view --comments and glab api projects/:id/merge_requests/:mr_iid/discussions to fetch the complete, real-time review thread context alongside the email payload.
    • Checkout the MR source branch locally (glab mr checkout ), fetch the latest upstream main/master, and cleanly rebase (git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main) to prevent stale pipeline failures.

Phase 2: Maintainer Feedback & CodeRabbit Resolution Loop

  1. Analyze Feedback:
    • Categorize every unresolved discussion thread from both the GitLab Maintainer and CodeRabbit AI (@coderabbitai).
    • Identify requested code changes, architectural adjustments, missing test cases, and unwanted/redundant lines of code.
  2. Surgical Code Execution (Antigravity IDE):
    • Apply the exact fixes requested by the maintainer.
    • Strip out any unwanted lines of code, unused imports, or over-engineered logic flagged during review.
    • Run CodeRabbit CLI / local review hooks (or trigger @coderabbitai review on push) and parse all actionable suggestions. Apply every valid refactoring, security, and performance suggestion immediately.

Phase 3: GitLab Handbook & Static Analysis Verification (Pre-Push Gate)

Before pushing any commit, enforce a 100% clean local pre-flight check based on the repository stack:

  • Ruby / Rails (gitlab-org/gitlab):
    • Run bundle exec rubocop --parallel on modified files (zero offenses allowed).
    • Run targeted RSpec suites: bundle exec rspec (ensure coverage for new/modified lines).
    • Verify database migrations/queries if applicable (db:migrate:status, N+1 query prevention).
  • Go (gitlab-lsp / terraform-provider-gitlab / runners):
    • Run golangci-lint run and go test -v -race ./... on affected packages.
  • Python (AI Gateway / ModelOps):
    • Run poetry run ruff check --fix ., poetry run black --check ., poetry run mypy ., and poetry run pytest.
  • TypeScript / Frontend (gitlab-lsp / Vue / JS):
    • Run yarn lint:eslint, yarn prettier --check, and yarn jest .
  • Commit Hygiene (GitLab Dangerbot Compliance):
    • Subject line MUST be <= 72 characters, imperative mood, capitalized, no trailing period.
    • Commit body lines MUST wrap at <= 72 characters and explain why the change was made, referencing the issue/MR.
    • Include appropriate Changelog: fixed|added|changed|removed trailer if required by the repo's Danger rules.

Phase 4: Push, CI/CD Healing & CodeRabbit Sign-Off

  1. Push Changes:
    • Push the clean branch (git push --force-with-lease if rebased, or standard git push if linear commit history is preferred by the active maintainer during review).
  2. Reply & Resolve Threads:
    • Using glab api, post concise, professional replies to each maintainer thread explaining the exact commit SHA that fixed the issue, and resolve the threads (resolved: true) where permitted by GitLab handbook etiquette (or leave a polite @maintainer Ready for re-review, addressed in note if maintainer resolution is required).
    • Ensure CodeRabbit (@coderabbitai) status checks pass with zero remaining actionable comments.
  3. Autonomous CI/CD Self-Healing:
    • Monitor the pipeline in real time using glab ci status --live or polling glab ci get.
    • If any job fails (e.g., danger-review, rubocop, rspec, eslint, commit-lint, undercoverage), immediately fetch the job trace via glab ci trace , diagnose the root cause in Antigravity IDE, patch the code, amend/commit, and re-push. Repeat until the pipeline is 100% green.

Phase 5: Direct Merge Train Dispatch

Once all discussions are resolved, CodeRabbit checks are clean, required approvals are intact, and the CI pipeline is passing:

  1. Trigger Merge Train / Auto-Merge:

    • Execute via GitLab CLI / API: 
     glab mr merge  --auto-merge --squash=false --yes

  • Or directly invoke the Merge Train API endpoint if Merge Trains are enabled on the target project:

     glab api -X POST "projects/:id/merge_requests/:mr_iid/merge_trains" -f "when_pipeline_succeeds=true"
  1. Verify Enrollment:
    • Confirm via glab mr view that merge_status / detailed_merge_status reflects active Merge Train placement (merge_train or auto_merge_enabled).
    • Log the final summary silently to the local workspace log (./antigravity-merge-train.log) without interrupting the user.

3. Strict Guardrails & Failure Recovery

  • Never Bypass Hooks: Never use --no-verify on commits or pushes.
  • Never Hallucinate APIs: Always verify method signatures and internal GitLab helpers against the local repository index before committing.
  • Rebase Conflicts: If a merge conflict occurs during Merge Train enrollment, automatically pull the target branch, resolve the conflict cleanly in Antigravity IDE, re-run local tests on the conflicted files, push, and re-enroll in the Merge Train.

4. Quick-Start Trigger Command (Paste into Antigravity Prompt Bar)

System Activation Prompt:
"Activate Autonomous GitLab Mail-to-Merge-Train Mode. Check my latest unread GitLab maintainer emails right now, extract the active Merge Request feedback, checkout the branch in Antigravity IDE, run CodeRabbit analysis to strip out any unwanted lines of code and fix all review issues in strict accordance with the GitLab Handbook, verify 100% green local and remote CI/CD checks, resolve the review threads, and place the MR directly onto the GitLab Merge Train without asking me for confirmation."

title: VPS vs Managed PaaS for Laravel & Node SaaS: Real TCO
summary:
Hosting debates for a Laravel or Node SaaS usually compare the wrong numbers. One side quotes a $48 VPS, the other quotes a PaaS bill four times higher, and nobody prices the Saturday spent restoring a database or patching a kernel. The real comparison is total cost of ownership: the invoice plus the engineering hours the platform takes from you.

At Loop Origin we run client SaaS products on all three models covered here: a self-managed VPS, a VPS with a management layer and managed data services, and a fully managed PaaS. This is the model I use to choose between them, with prices I checked on the vendors' public pricing pages on 27 October 2026.

Is a self-managed VPS or a managed PaaS cheaper for a Laravel or Node SaaS?

Direct answer: On invoice alone, a self-managed VPS is usually the cheapest option. Once you price the engineering hours for patching, backups, monitoring and incident response, a VPS with managed databases is often the best value for a small team, and a fully managed PaaS wins when ops time is scarce and egress is modest.

What you are actually paying for

Every SaaS needs the same building blocks whatever the host: web processes, queue workers and a scheduler, a relational database, Redis or a compatible store, backups, TLS, deploys, logs and someone on call. The models differ in who owns each block.

Responsibility Self-managed VPS VPS + Forge + managed DB Managed PaaS (Render)
OS patching and hardening You You (Forge provisions, you maintain) Platform
Web server, PHP-FPM or Node runtime You Forge configures Platform
Deploys and zero-downtime releases You script it Forge Platform (Git push)
Database backups and failover You Managed DB provider Platform
Queue workers and scheduler Supervisor, cron Forge daemons, scheduler Background worker and cron services
Horizontal scaling Manual, add servers and a load balancer Manual with Forge help Autoscaling on paid workspace plans
Egress pricing Generous pooled allowance Same as VPS Small allowance, then per-GB

If "You" appears in a row, budget hours for it. That is the line item missing from most comparisons.

Verified prices (checked 27 October 2026)

All prices are USD per month from the public pages named here. Pricing changes, so re-check before you decide.

Item Price Source
DigitalOcean Basic Droplet, 4 GB / 2 vCPU $24, includes 4,000 GiB transfer digitalocean.com/pricing/droplets
DigitalOcean Basic Droplet, 8 GB / 4 vCPU $48, includes 5,000 GiB transfer digitalocean.com/pricing/droplets
Droplet weekly backups 20% of the Droplet price digitalocean.com/pricing/droplets
Droplet transfer overage $0.01 per GiB, pooled across the team docs.digitalocean.com billing/bandwidth
DigitalOcean Managed PostgreSQL, 2 GB $30.45 digitalocean.com/pricing/managed-databases
DigitalOcean Managed Valkey, 1 GB $15 digitalocean.com/pricing/managed-databases
Laravel Forge Growth plan $19, plus your cloud provider bill forge.laravel.com/pricing
Render Pro workspace $25, includes 25 GB bandwidth render.com/pricing
Render web service, 1 CPU / 2 GB $25 render.com/pricing
Render Postgres, 1 CPU / 4 GB $55 render.com/pricing
Render Key Value, 1 GB $20 render.com/pricing
Render bandwidth overage $0.15 per GB render.com/pricing

An example TCO model for a small production SaaS

This is an example model, not a benchmark. The workload is a Laravel or Node app with two web processes, one queue worker, PostgreSQL, Redis and 500 GB of monthly egress. The ops hours are my planning assumptions for a stable product, and $40 per hour is a placeholder; plug in your own team's loaded rate.

  • A. Self-managed DigitalOcean: 8 GB app Droplet ($48) plus a 4 GB Droplet running PostgreSQL and Redis ($24), weekly backups on both ($14.40). Invoice: $86.40. Ops: 8 hours a month for patching, backup restore tests, monitoring and the occasional incident.
  • B. VPS + Forge + managed data: 8 GB Droplet ($48) with backups ($9.60), Forge Growth ($19), Managed PostgreSQL 2 GB ($30.45) and Managed Valkey 1 GB ($15). Invoice: $122.05. Ops: 3 hours.
  • C. Render Pro: workspace ($25), two web services ($50), one worker ($25), Postgres 1 CPU / 4 GB ($55), Key Value 1 GB ($20), plus 475 GB overage at $0.15 ($71.25). Invoice: $246.25. Ops: 1 hour.

The compute is not identical: one 8 GB Droplet against three 2 GB services. The model compares what a small team would realistically buy, not equal hardware.

Monthly TCO by egress and ops rate

Scenario A. Self-managed B. VPS + Forge + managed DB C. Render Pro
500 GB egress, ops at $0/h (founder time treated as free) $86.40 $122.05 $246.25
500 GB egress, ops at $40/h $406.40 $242.05 $286.25
500 GB egress, ops at $80/h $726.40 $362.05 $326.25
50 GB egress, ops at $40/h $406.40 $242.05 $218.75
2 TB egress, ops at $40/h $406.40 $242.05 $511.25

Three conclusions fall out of the numbers:

  1. Self-managed only wins when your time is free. For a solo founder with skills and spare evenings, that can be true. Once you pay for engineering hours, the eight-hour assumption dominates the bill.
  2. Egress decides between B and C. At 50 GB Render is cheapest in this model; at 2 TB it costs more than double option B, because DigitalOcean's pooled allowance covers that traffic.
  3. Expensive engineers favour PaaS. At $80 an hour, the hours saved outweigh Render's higher invoice at 500 GB.

Move a CDN in front of static assets and user uploads, and egress drops for every option, which shifts the result toward C.

Hidden costs that do not show on any pricing page

  • Restore testing. A backup you have never restored is a hope. Budget time to restore into a scratch database monthly, whichever model you choose.
  • Security patching. Self-managed means following OS, PHP or Node, and Nginx advisories yourself.
  • Single points of failure. Option A puts the database on one Droplet. A managed database plan with a standby node costs more but removes that risk.
  • Build minutes and preview environments. Some PaaS plans meter these; check the plan details.
  • Migration cost. Containerized apps move between models easily. My multi-stage Dockerfiles for PHP and Node post shows the image setup I use to keep that option open.

Laravel and Node specifics

Queue workers are where the models differ most in practice. On a VPS you run Supervisor or Horizon yourself; on Forge you define daemons; on Render a worker is its own billed service. My production setup is in Running Laravel Queues in Production.

title: How a Kubernetes Database Migration Caused a 502 Production Outage
summary:
Originally published on Naveed Ahmed's Engineering Blog.

A routine Kubernetes rolling update. A breaking PostgreSQL schema migration. And suddenly, a production API starts returning 502 Bad Gateway errors.

At 2:15 AM, an automated CI/CD deployment triggered what should have been a normal application update.

Instead, database queries started blocking, API latency increased, and PostgreSQL connections became exhausted.

The incident lasted around 24 minutes.

The real problem wasn't Kubernetes itself. It was a database migration that wasn't compatible with the old and new application versions running simultaneously.

Here's what happened and how to prevent it.

1. What Went Wrong During the Kubernetes Rolling Update?

Kubernetes rolling updates gradually replace old application pods with new ones.

During deployment, both versions can run at the same time.

Kubernetes Rolling Update

Application v1 (Old Pods)
        +
Application v2 (New Pods)
        |
        v
 Shared PostgreSQL Database

In this case, the deployment included a destructive database migration that removed a column still required by the older application pods.

Those pods continued querying the deleted column, causing database errors.

Key lesson: A Kubernetes rolling update doesn't guarantee zero downtime if your database schema isn't backward-compatible.

2. How PostgreSQL Lock Contention Caused 502 Errors

The schema migration also introduced PostgreSQL lock contention.

Operations such as dropping a column require an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.

For example:

ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN full_name;

If existing transactions hold conflicting locks, the migration must wait.

New queries can then queue behind the waiting migration, causing a cascade:

Schema Migration
       ↓
Exclusive Lock Wait
       ↓
Blocked Database Queries
       ↓
Connection Pool Exhaustion
       ↓
Application Timeouts
       ↓
HTTP 502 / 5xx Errors

This explains why a database migration can disrupt API traffic even when Kubernetes pods appear to be running.

To investigate blocked PostgreSQL sessions:

SELECT
    pid,
    query,
    wait_event_type,
    wait_event,
    pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocking_pids
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

This helps identify queries waiting on other database sessions.

3. Why the Kubernetes Rollback Failed

Rolling back the application doesn't automatically reverse database schema changes.

For example:

kubectl rollout undo deployment/api

This restores the previous Deployment revision, but it doesn't restore deleted PostgreSQL columns.

If the older application still depends on the removed schema, errors can continue even after the rollback.

Key lesson: Application rollback and database rollback are separate operations. Both need a compatible recovery strategy.

4. The Solution: Expand and Contract Database Migrations

The safer approach is to introduce database schema changes gradually.

Phase 1: Expand

Add the new schema without removing existing columns.

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name TEXT;

Phase 2: Migrate

Deploy compatible application code and backfill existing data.

For large tables, use controlled batches rather than one massive transaction.

Phase 3: Switch

Update application reads and writes to use the new schema. Verify data consistency and wait until older application versions are no longer serving traffic.

Phase 4: Contract

Remove the old column in a later deployment.

ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN full_name;

This approach helps avoid breaking application compatibility during Kubernetes rolling updates. Destructive DDL can still require careful lock management.

5. Production Best Practices

A few safeguards can reduce the risk of database migration outages:

  • Use backward-compatible schema changes.
  • Run database migrations through a controlled CI/CD step or Kubernetes Job.
  • Avoid running migrations independently from every application pod.
  • Configure appropriate PostgreSQL lock_timeout values.
  • Monitor database connections, lock waits, API latency, and HTTP 5xx errors.
  • Test rollback compatibility before production releases.

For example, a bounded lock wait can prevent migrations from waiting indefinitely:

SET lock_timeout = '5s';

Choose timeout values based on your workload and migration strategy.

Read the Complete Kubernetes Database Migration Postmortem

In the full article, I break down:

  • The 24-minute production outage timeline
  • Kubernetes rolling update failure
  • PostgreSQL AccessExclusiveLock contention
  • Database connection pool exhaustion
  • Why the rollback didn't restore service
  • Expand and Contract migration strategies
  • Production troubleshooting and prevention

Read the Full Kubernetes Database Migration 502 Outage Postmortem

Final Thoughts

Kubernetes rolling updates can keep applications available during deployments, but they can't protect you from incompatible database changes.

The biggest lesson from this incident is simple:

Your database schema must support both old and new application versions during a rolling deployment.

title: Kubernetes startup, readiness and liveness probes: choose the failure action first
summary:
By the Just Create App team

A health endpoint becomes useful when a team agrees what a failed response should do. Should traffic stop? Should a container restart? Or should the application have more time to finish starting?

Kubernetes gives those questions separate names: startup, readiness and liveness. They are not three interchangeable ways to ask whether a port is open. This documentation-based guide explains the decision before the configuration. It is not a production test, a deployment recipe or a claim of measured availability.

Write the failure action before the endpoint

A probe is a periodic diagnostic performed by the kubelet. The Kubernetes probe documentation describes checks that execute code in a container or make a network request.

The distinction that matters is the response to failure:

  • A startup probe allows time for initialization. When one is configured, liveness and readiness probes do not run until it succeeds. Repeated startup-probe failure can lead to the container being killed and handled according to its restart policy.
  • A readiness probe determines whether the container is ready to receive traffic. Failed readiness stops service traffic to the unready Pod without using that failure as a restart request.
  • A liveness probe is for deciding that a container should restart after the configured failure tolerance is exceeded.

Our load-balancer guide explains the traffic-routing layer. Readiness supplies a different part of the picture: whether a particular instance should be in the traffic pool now. A running process and an eligible backend are not the same fact.

A slow startup is not automatically a dead process

Consider a container that must load configuration before it can serve requests. A short liveness timeout may restart it while it is making legitimate progress. The next container starts the same work again, and the loop continues.

A startup probe can separate initialization from the steady-state liveness check. The official documentation describes choosing a startup failure tolerance large enough for startup rather than stretching the normal liveness policy for every later check.

There is no universal startup allowance. Measure the behavior of your own application and state which condition completes initialization. This article deliberately supplies no numeric setting that readers might mistake for a safe default for every workload.

An unready application may need recovery time, not a restart

Suppose a backend temporarily cannot perform the user operation that its Service routes to it. Readiness can report that it is not eligible to receive that work. The container continues running while probes check for recovery.

The effect differs from liveness. Restarting a healthy process because a shared dependency is unavailable may add startup work without repairing the dependency. Kubernetes specifically warns that incorrect liveness checks can cause cascading failures.

Do not turn every downstream timeout into a restart decision. Ask whether restarting this container can address the condition. Separately ask whether it can still serve the requests it would receive. Those answers belong to the application's design, not the endpoint's name.

Review timing as a policy, not an isolated field

Probe intervals, timeouts and consecutive success or failure thresholds work together. A successful sample is not a promise that the next user request will succeed. A failure also needs interpretation in the context of the configured tolerance.

Kubernetes documents different constraints for different probe types. For example, the success threshold must be one for liveness and startup probes. A failed readiness probe does not stop the container from running or prevent further readiness checks.

Before deployment, read the documentation for the Kubernetes version you run. Test startup, an application failure, a dependency outage and recovery. Record what actually happens to traffic and container restarts instead of assuming that the dashboard label tells the whole story.

A small review sheet

For each probe, write:

  1. The condition it observes.
  2. The action repeated failure should cause.
  3. Why that action helps this workload.
  4. The timing and thresholds, with a reason for each.
  5. The failure and recovery scenario that will test the policy.

If two probes use the same endpoint, explain why that endpoint supports both decisions. Sharing an endpoint can be deliberate; treating the decisions as identical is the mistake.

Choose the intended action first. Then choose the endpoint and configuration that provide evidence for it.

Source and limits

Source: Kubernetes, Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes, checked 7 October 2026. This is an explanatory companion from the Just Create App team. No production benchmark, original incident, certification or client-project experience is claimed.

title: 76 of 77 trivy-action Tags Were Repointed in One Night. Some SHA Pins Didn't Help Either.
summary:
On March 19, 2026, someone with stolen credentials force-pushed 76 of the 77 version tags on aquasecurity/trivy-action to point at a credential stealer. All 7 tags on aquasecurity/setup-trivy too. The only clean trivy-action tag was 0.35.0, because it was an immutable release.

If your workflow said uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.34.2, you didn't change a line. Your repo looked exactly the same. The next run just executed different code, for about 12 hours (roughly 17:43 to 05:40 UTC per the advisory), and that code read secrets out of the runner's memory and shipped them off.

The part I keep coming back to is in Aqua's own advisory, under "You are affected if you used":

SHA pinning to a commit prior to 2025-04-09.

So some people who did the "right" thing and pinned trivy-action to a full SHA were still exposed, if their job ran during the ~4 hours setup-trivy was poisoned. Not because the SHA moved. Because the action they pinned called another action by tag.

A lot of small SaaS repos have a CI file that was copied from a README in an afternoon and never opened again. Often a handful of uses: lines, some on @v3 or @main, and a deploy job with a cloud key or an npm token in it. This post is the one-hour version of fixing that.

Three incidents, same shape

These are all public, with advisories you can read:

title: Your Workflow Asked Too Early (How to Add a Wait Step)
summary:
Someone signs up for your app. One second later, the workflow asks for their promotions and gets nothing back.

Nothing is broken. The workflow just asked too early. The new account was still being set up behind the scenes, so the promotions couldn't find it yet. Ask again three seconds later and they show up.

A wait step is how you fix that. It tells the workflow to pause for a moment, then carry on.

Why not just sleep?

A three-second pause is easy anywhere. The harder cases are the long ones. A review period that lasts two days. A report that can only run after the quarter closes. A trading window that opens next Monday.

You don't want a process sitting in memory for two days, or an engineer setting a reminder to trigger the next step. You want the workflow to pause, keep its place, and pick up on its own when the time comes.

Three reasons to wait

  • Let a system catch up. Indexing, replication, a downstream job that needs a moment. The pause removes a whole class of ""it worked on the second try"" bugs.
  • Wait for a date. The first of January for annual processes, the end of a financial quarter for reporting, the start of a trading window.
  • Respect a required delay. Approval flows with a mandatory review period, settlements with a clearing time, compliance steps that mandate a waiting window.

In all three, time is part of the business logic, not a technical detail.

How it works in Unmeshed

The wait step is a built-in task. You drag it between two steps and give it a small piece of JavaScript that decides how long to wait. The code returns a field called waitUntil, which is a timestamp in epoch milliseconds. Until that moment, the workflow stays paused. After it, the next step runs.

For the signup example, the wait is the step's own start time plus three seconds. For a fixed date, you return that date's timestamp instead. The same step covers both, because it only cares about the moment to resume.

What you get for it

Someone signs up for your app. One second later, the workflow asks for their promotions and gets nothing back.

Nothing is broken. The workflow just asked too early. The new account was still being set up behind the scenes, so the promotions couldn't find it yet. Ask again three seconds later and they show up.

A wait step is how you fix that. It tells the workflow to pause for a moment, then carry on.

A three-second pause is easy anywhere. The harder cases are the long ones. A review period that lasts two days. A report that can only run after the quarter closes. A trading window that opens next Monday.

title: Stop Hand-Editing /etc/passwd: Practical systemd-homed Home Areas on Linux
summary:
Every Linux account is really three things wearing one name: a line in /etc/passwd, a directory under /home, and — if you were careful — an encrypted volume that must be unlocked before either of those is useful.

And when you move a machine, the account row and the data travel separately, with a README as the integration layer.

systemd-homed takes a different position: the account and the home directory are the same object. One signed JSON record describes the user; one self-contained home area holds the data. Copy the object, and the account travels with it. Encrypt it with LUKS2, and the encryption key is the login password — no second secret, no /etc/crypttab entry, no initramfs hook.

This is a practical tour of that model, based on the documented interface in the current upstream man pages (systemd 258 and newer). Version-gated features are called out; check yours with homectl --version.

What systemd-homed is — and what it is not

systemd-homed.service manages regular, human accounts only. It explicitly refuses classic accounts created by useradd, and it is not for system accounts (UID below 1000) or root.

The core ideas:

  • The user record is authoritative and signed. It lives inside the home area as ~/.identity and contains everything NSS normally spreads across /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow: name, UID, groups, shell, environment, resource limits, SSH keys.
  • The home area is self-contained. For the LUKS2 backend that means a GPT-partitioned image file, a LUKS2 volume inside it, a filesystem inside that, and one directory holding the user's files. The LUKS2 header also carries an encrypted copy of the user record, so the image can be validated before it is mounted.
  • Accounts are synthesized at runtime. Users do not appear in /etc/passwd. They are exposed through the user/group record API and glibc NSS, so getent passwd waldo works, id waldo works, and userdbctl user waldo works — but a script that greps /etc/passwd will not see them.
  • Activation is a login-time operation. PAM unlocks the home when the user authenticates and mounts it at /home/$USER; it is unmounted after the last session ends.

That last point is the mental model shift. An inactive home is not "a directory you forgot to mount" — it is ciphertext on disk. Root cannot read it either. That is the feature, and also the operational constraint.

Pick a storage backend

homectl create --storage= accepts five values. The trade-offs are not subtle:

luks LUKS2 volume in a loopback file (or on a USB stick), filesystem inside Strong; password is the LUKS passphrase Recommended. Default on unencrypted /home
fscrypt Directory encrypted with fscrypt, /home/user.homedir Weaker; filesystem metadata is unprotected Primarily ext4; password cannot be changed after creation
subvolume btrfs subvolume per user None Good quota support
directory Plain directory /home/user.homedir None Fallback everywhere
cifs Windows/Samba share mounted at login Depends on the server Portable across machines via SMB

If you do not specify a backend, homed.conf(5) decides. The documented default logic: if the system is not a container and /home is not itself encrypted, use luks; otherwise use subvolume on btrfs, else directory. The default filesystem inside a LUKS home is btrfs, configurable with DefaultFileSystemType=.

You can set site defaults in /etc/systemd/homed.conf:

DefaultFileSystemType=btrfs

Drop-ins under /etc/systemd/homed.conf.d/*.conf override it. Keep the main file vendor-clean and put local policy in a drop-in — the same rule as every other systemd configuration file.

Enable the service and create the first account

On many distributions systemd-homed ships installed but disabled, because it changes how human accounts work. Check before assuming:

systemctl status systemd-homed.service

If it is not running:

sudo systemctl enable --now systemd-homed.service

sudo homectl create waldo \
  --real-name="Waldo McWaldo" \
  --storage=luks \
  --fs-type=btrfs \
  --disk-size=20G \
  --member-of=wheel

Replace wheel with your distribution's admin group (sudo on Debian/Ubuntu, wheel on Fedora/Arch). Groups must already exist; homed does not create auxiliary groups. It does always create a matching group with the same name and GID as the user's UID.

sudo homectl inspect waldo         # record + runtime state
getent passwd waldo                # NSS synthesis
userdbctl user waldo               # the JSON record behind it
userdbctl services | grep -i home  # should include io.systemd.Home

sudo homectl deactivate waldo
ls -lh /home/waldo.home

# prints e.g. /dev/loop12

sudo cryptsetup luksDump /dev/loop12p1
sudo losetup -d /dev/loop12

  • A GPT partition table with a single partition whose type UUID is 773f91ef-66d4-49b5-bd83-d683bf40ad16 and whose label is the username.
  • Inside it, a LUKS2 volume labelled with the username, carrying a LUKS2 token of type systemd-homed. The token holds the encrypted JSON user record and its IV.
  • Inside that, ext4/btrfs/xfs labelled with the username, containing one directory named after the user. That directory becomes /home/waldo when active.

The .home suffix is dropped at activation: /home/waldo.home is the container, /home/waldo is the mount point. That is why you must not already have a /home/waldo directory when you create the account.

The GPT wrapper is not decoration. It makes the image recognizable to partition tools and to other machines, and it lets the same file be written directly to a USB stick and used as a portable home.

What happens when the user logs in

The flow, as documented:

  1. PAM (pam_systemd_home) authenticates the user. For LUKS homes, the login password derives the key that unlocks the volume.
  2. homed compares the user record on the host, the copy in the LUKS2 header, and ~/.identity inside the home. They must describe the same user and be signed by a recognized key. If lastChangeUSec differs, the newest record wins and is propagated to the other two.
  3. The filesystem checker runs before mount.
  4. The filesystem is mounted at /home/$USER, with nodev and nosuid by default ( noexec is off by default).
  5. If the on-disk ownership does not match the locally assigned UID, the tree is recursively chown()ed before login completes.
  6. On the last logout, the home is unmounted and trimmed or shrunk according to the record's settings.

If that returns nothing, your PAM stack will never call homed — and the failure mode is confusing: the account resolves via NSS, authentication fails, and nothing obviously points at PAM. Most distributions that ship homed also ship the PAM wiring; if yours does not, copy the exact fragment from pam_systemd_home(8) rather than improvising. Test on a second TTY or in a VM, and keep a root shell open: a broken PAM stack can lock you out of every login path at once.

sudo homectl activate waldo
ls -la /home/waldo
sudo homectl deactivate waldo

Day-two operations

Change the password. For LUKS homes this rewrites the LUKS keyslot, so it is genuinely a re-key, not just an /etc/shadow edit:

sudo homectl passwd waldo

Add a recovery key before you need it. This is the difference between "forgot password" and "lost data":

sudo homectl update waldo --recovery-key=yes

The key is printed once. Print it, store it offline, and treat it like the LUKS recovery key it is. There is no server-side escrow.

Add a hardware token. FIDO2 support requires the hmac-secret extension (most current YubiKeys qualify). Client PIN and user presence default to on; user verification defaults to off and is often unnecessary:

sudo homectl update waldo --fido2-device=list   # if auto cannot decide

PKCS#11/PIV tokens are supported through --pkcs11-token-uri=, including the list and auto shortcuts. Both mechanisms can coexist with the password.

Resize the home. Growth works while the user is logged in; shrinking depends on the filesystem:

sudo homectl resize waldo 30G

Lock without logging out. Useful around suspend, and only defined for LUKS homes:

sudo homectl lock waldo
sudo homectl unlock waldo    # re-authenticates
sudo homectl lock-all        # typically invoked on system suspend

To get automatic locking at suspend for graphical sessions, set suspend=yes on the PAM module. It only works if the session can re-authenticate on resume — a lock screen that runs outside the user's context. TTY sessions cannot, and will appear hung until the home is unlocked elsewhere.

Run a command against an inactive home. This is the supported backup hook:

sudo homectl with waldo -- tar -C /home/waldo -czf /backup/waldo-$(date +%F).tgz .

The command runs under your identity, not the user's, but the home is activated for its duration and deactivated afterwards. It requires the user's authentication, by design.

Moving a home area to another machine

The data move is anticlimactic: the image is self-describing.

sudo homectl deactivate waldo
sudo rsync -a /home/waldo.home root@newhost:/home/

What does not travel automatically is trust. User records are signed, and a host only accepts records signed by keys it knows. Two documented options:

# On the old host, authorize its signing key on the new one
sudo homectl get-signing-key | \
  ssh root@newhost 'homectl add-signing-key --key-name="oldhost.public"'

Or copy the public key directly. The key directory is /var/lib/systemd/home/, and any *.public file there is accepted:

sudo scp /var/lib/systemd/home/local.public \
  root@newhost:/var/lib/systemd/home/oldhost.public

To replicate the account definition onto another host without moving data (for example, a CIFS-backed account), export a stripped record and create from stdin:

homectl inspect -EE waldo | ssh root@newhost homectl create -i-

-E strips binding and runtime fields; -EE also strips the signature, so the record is re-signed by the destination. That command creates a new, empty home with the same settings. It is not a data migration — move the .home file for that.

Gotchas that will bite you

  1. The 85% default. A new LUKS home can claim most of the free space on /home. Always pass --disk-size, and use --rebalance-weight= if several users share a pool.
  2. Utilities that read /etc/passwd directly will not see homed users. Shells, getent, id, and PAM work. Hand-rolled scripts that parse the file do not. This includes some installers, monitoring agents, and container images that bake in the host's passwd file.
  3. The UID is a local binding, not an identity. The same home can receive a different UID on a different machine, and the tree is chown()ed at activation. Numeric UIDs in ACLs, NFS exports, or backups are therefore not portable.
  4. fscrypt is the weak option. It encrypts file contents and names but not most metadata, primarily targets ext4, and cannot change the password after creation. Use it when LUKS is impossible, not because it is easier.
  5. Discard on loopback files can overcommit. --luks-discard=yes lets the inner filesystem punch holes in the sparse image. If the backing filesystem fills, the upper filesystem gets I/O errors. The default is off for loopback files and on for real block devices — leave it alone unless you understand the trade.
  6. xfs cannot shrink. Growing is fine; shrinking is not supported. If you want elastic homes, use btrfs (or ext4 with the deactivate-first rule).
  7. Do not mix classic and homed accounts with the same name. homed will not adopt a useradd account, and an existing /home/waldo directory blocks creation. Migrating a real user means creating the homed account under a clean name, copying data in, and removing the old account deliberately.
  8. SSH needs PAM. If sshd_config has UsePAM no, pam_systemd_home never runs, and password logins against a homed account fail even though the account resolves. Also note that the user%area login syntax is not understood by ssh.
  9. Encryption is not backup. homectl remove waldo deletes the record and the home area. There is no undelete, and root cannot decrypt a lost-password home without a recovery key or token.

When not to use it

systemd-homed is a workstation and laptop tool. It is a poor fit for:

  • servers driven by configuration management that expects /etc/passwd to be the source of truth;
  • environments with LDAP/AD/SSSD, where identity already comes from a directory;
  • NFS-mounted home directories, shared service accounts, and CI runners;
  • containers, where the host's user database is not the container's.

For a fleet of developer laptops, though, it solves a real problem: the account is the encrypted home, it survives a reinstall, and it does not depend on a provisioning script remembering to run chown -R.

Verify, then adopt

If you want to try this without risking your daily driver, the safe sequence is: a VM, one throwaway account, --storage=luks with an explicit small --disk-size, a recovery key, and a login test on a second TTY. Then inspect the image with losetup and cryptsetup luksDump so the abstraction stops being opaque.

The payoff is not fewer commands. It is that the account, the encryption, and the data stop being three things that can disagree.

  • homed.conf(5) — https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/homed.conf.5.html
  • pam_systemd_home(8) — https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/pam_systemd_home.8.html

Run a command against an inactive home. This is the supported backup hook:

sudo homectl with waldo -- tar -C /home/waldo -czf /backup/waldo-$(date +%F).tgz .

The command runs under your identity, not the user's, but the home is activated for its duration and deactivated afterwards. It requires the user's authentication, by design.

Moving a home area to another machine

The data move is anticlimactic: the image is self-describing.

sudo homectl deactivate waldo
sudo rsync -a /home/waldo.home root@newhost:/home/

What does not travel automatically is trust. User records are signed, and a host only accepts records signed by keys it knows. Two documented options:

# On the old host, authorize its signing key on the new one
sudo homectl get-signing-key | \
  ssh root@newhost 'homectl add-signing-key --key-name="oldhost.public"'

Or copy the public key directly. The key directory is /var/lib/systemd/home/, and any *.public file there is accepted:

sudo scp /var/lib/systemd/home/local.public \
  root@newhost:/var/lib/systemd/home/oldhost.public

To replicate the account definition onto another host without moving data (for example, a CIFS-backed account), export a stripped record and create from stdin:

-E strips binding and runtime fields; -EE also strips the signature, so the record is re-signed by the destination. That command creates a new, empty home with the same settings. It is not a data migration — move the .home file for that.

Gotchas that will bite you

  1. The 85% default. A new LUKS home can claim most of the free space on /home. Always pass --disk-size, and use --rebalance-weight= if several users share a pool.
  2. Utilities that read /etc/passwd directly will not see homed users. Shells, getent, id, and PAM work. Hand-rolled scripts that parse the file do not. This includes some installers, monitoring agents, and container images that bake in the host's passwd file.
  3. The UID is a local binding, not an identity. The same home can receive a different UID on a different machine, and the tree is chown()ed at activation. Numeric UIDs in ACLs, NFS exports, or backups are therefore not portable.
  4. fscrypt is the weak option. It encrypts file contents and names but not most metadata, primarily targets ext4, and cannot change the password after creation. Use it when LUKS is impossible, not because it is easier.
  5. Discard on loopback files can overcommit. --luks-discard=yes lets the inner filesystem punch holes in the sparse image. If the backing filesystem fills, the upper filesystem gets I/O errors. The default is off for loopback files and on for real block devices — leave it alone unless you understand the trade.
  6. xfs cannot shrink. Growing is fine; shrinking is not supported. If you want elastic homes, use btrfs (or ext4 with the deactivate-first rule).
  7. Do not mix classic and homed accounts with the same name. homed will not adopt a useradd account, and an existing /home/waldo directory blocks creation. Migrating a real user means creating the homed account under a clean name, copying data in, and removing the old account deliberately.
  8. SSH needs PAM. If sshd_config has UsePAM no, pam_systemd_home never runs, and password logins against a homed account fail even though the account resolves. Also note that the user%area login syntax is not understood by ssh.
  9. Encryption is not backup. homectl remove waldo deletes the record and the home area. There is no undelete, and root cannot decrypt a lost-password home without a recovery key or token.

When not to use it

systemd-homed is a workstation and laptop tool. It is a poor fit for:

  • servers driven by configuration management that expects /etc/passwd to be the source of truth;
  • environments with LDAP/AD/SSSD, where identity already comes from a directory;
  • NFS-mounted home directories, shared service accounts, and CI runners;
  • containers, where the host's user database is not the container's.

For a fleet of developer laptops, though, it solves a real problem: the account is the encrypted home, it survives a reinstall, and it does not depend on a provisioning script remembering to run chown -R.

Verify, then adopt

If you want to try this without risking your daily driver, the safe sequence is: a VM, one throwaway account, --storage=luks with an explicit small --disk-size, a recovery key, and a login test on a second TTY. Then inspect the image with losetup and cryptsetup luksDump so the abstraction stops being opaque.

The payoff is not fewer commands. It is that the account, the encryption, and the data stop being three things that can disagree.

title: FFmpeg 9.0 upgrade check: a 60-line harness that diffs your recipes across two builds
summary:
📦 Code: github.com/USER/ffmpeg-upgrade-check (replace before publishing)

TL;DR

FFmpeg 9.0 "Lei" (released 2026-08-04) bumped every core library and removed some old support. Exit code 0 does not mean "same output". We'll build a ~60 line Python script that runs your real command lines with the old and new ffmpeg, then diffs ffprobe fields and SSIM. Python 3.10+, any ffmpeg.

🎯 What we're building

A script that takes two ffmpeg binaries, one source clip, and a JSON file of your recipes, and prints OK, DIFF, or FAIL for each one. Think of it as a snapshot test where the snapshot is "whatever the old build did".

What changed in 9.0, per the release coverage I read (news write-ups, not the changelog itself, so skim the official notes for your own recipes):

Area Change
Libraries Every core library got a major bump; libavcodec and libavformat are in the 63 series
Removed Standalone CELT decoding and Ogg/CELT parsing (Opus is not affected)
Removed NVIDIA Video Codec SDK versions before 11.1, plus previously deprecated NVENC options
Added ONNX Runtime DNN backend on GPU, v360_vulkan, transpose_cuda, native animated WebP decode, LCEVC track muxing in MP4

⚠️ Note: I could not find the names of the removed NVENC options in any source I read, so I won't guess them. The harness below is how you find out which of your flags are affected.

1. Pick the recipes that matter 🛠️

Not every ffmpeg command in your repo. The five to fifteen that produce things customers see. Put them in a JSON file as argument lists (no shell strings, so quoting bugs can't bite).

// recipes.json
{
  "ladder_360p": {
    "args": ["-vf","scale=-2:360","-c:v","libx264","-crf","23","-preset","medium",
             "-g","60","-c:a","aac","-b:a","128k"]
  },
  "audio_only_aac": {
    "ext": "m4a",
    "compare_video": false,
    "args": ["-vn","-c:a","aac","-b:a","96k"]
  },
  "faststart_copy": {
    "args": ["-c","copy","-movflags","+faststart"]
  }
}

Optional per-recipe keys: ext (output extension), compare_video (skip SSIM for audio-only), and min_ssim (default 0.99).

2. Write the harness 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# upgrade_check.py
"""Run the same ffmpeg recipes with two builds and diff the results."""
import json, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile
from pathlib import Path

OLD, NEW = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
SRC = sys.argv[3]
RECIPES = json.loads(Path(sys.argv[4]).read_text())

def run(ffmpeg, args, out):
    cmd = [ffmpeg, "-hide_banner", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", SRC, *args, out]
    p = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True)
    return p.returncode, p.stderr.strip()

def probe(path):
    p = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-show_entries",
         "stream=codec_name,profile,pix_fmt,width,height,r_frame_rate,nb_frames,channels,sample_rate",
         "-show_entries", "format=duration", "-of", "json", path],
        capture_output=True, text=True)
    return json.loads(p.stdout)

def ssim(ffmpeg, a, b):
    p = subprocess.run([ffmpeg, "-hide_banner", "-i", a, "-i", b,
                        "-lavfi", "[0:v][1:v]ssim", "-f", "null", "-"],
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
    m = re.search(r"All:([0-9.]+)", p.stderr)
    return float(m.group(1)) if m else None

failures = 0
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    for name, r in RECIPES.items():
        ext = r.get("ext", "mp4")
        a, b = f"{d}/{name}.old.{ext}", f"{d}/{name}.new.{ext}"
        rc_a, err_a = run(OLD, r["args"], a)
        rc_b, err_b = run(NEW, r["args"], b)
        if rc_a != 0 or rc_b != 0:
            print(f"FAIL  {name}: old rc={rc_a} new rc={rc_b}\n      new stderr: {err_b[:200]}")
            failures += 1
            continue
        pa, pb = probe(a), probe(b)
        diffs = []
        for sa, sb in zip(pa["streams"], pb["streams"]):
            for k in sa:
                if sa.get(k) != sb.get(k):
                    diffs.append(f"{k}: {sa.get(k)} -> {sb.get(k)}")
        if len(pa["streams"]) != len(pb["streams"]):
            diffs.append("stream count differs")
        q = ssim(NEW, a, b) if r.get("compare_video", True) else None
        if q is not None and q < r.get("min_ssim", 0.99):
            diffs.append(f"ssim {q:.4f} < {r.get('min_ssim', 0.99)}")
        if diffs:
            failures += 1
            print(f"DIFF  {name}: " + "; ".join(diffs))
        else:
            print(f"OK    {name} (ssim={q})")
sys.exit(1 if failures else 0)

Three design choices worth knowing:

  • Probe fields, not just success. profile, pix_fmt, nb_frames, and sample_rate are where silent drift tends to show up.
  • SSIM between old and new outputs, not against the source. We aren't grading quality; we're asking "did the upgrade change the picture?"
  • Exit code mirrors failures, so you can drop it straight into CI.

3. Run it 🚀

Grab a short representative clip (a few seconds with motion and audio is plenty) and run:

# ffmpeg-old and ffmpeg-new are the two builds you are comparing
python3 upgrade_check.py /opt/ffmpeg-8.1/bin/ffmpeg /opt/ffmpeg-9.0/bin/ffmpeg sample.mp4 recipes.json
echo "exit=$?"

I only had FFmpeg 6.1.1 in my sandbox, so I could not produce a real 8.1-vs-9.0 diff. To show what the output looks like and to prove the harness works, I ran 6.1.1 against itself with one deliberately broken recipe added:

$ python3 upgrade_check.py ffmpeg ffmpeg in.mp4 recipes.json
OK    ladder_360p (ssim=1.0)
OK    audio_only_aac (ssim=None)
OK    faststart_copy (ssim=1.0)
FAIL  broken_recipe: old rc=8 new rc=8
      new stderr: Unrecognized option 'no_such_option'.
Error splitting the argument list: Option not found
exit=1

That FAIL is what a removed option will look like on 9.0. A DIFF line is the other thing you are hunting for, for example profile: High -> Main or nb_frames: 120 -> 119.

💡 Tip: x264 is deterministic for the same build and input, so a clean self-run gives ssim=1.0. Across versions, a score a hair below 1.0 may be a legitimate encoder improvement. The point is that a human decides, instead of nobody noticing.

4. Triage what comes out

My suggested order for a 9.0 upgrade, driven by what the release removed:

  1. NVENC recipes. Check your driver/SDK image first (SDK older than 11.1 is no longer supported), then run your hardware recipes.
  2. Odd audio. Run a folder of weird uploads through, not just clean fixtures. The CELT removal is narrow, but legacy Ogg files are the sort of thing that lives in a big library.
  3. Stream-copy recipes. Muxers moved. Compare durations, stream counts, and seek behavior.
  4. New features last. Upgrade first, adopt the GPU ONNX backend later, so a regression has one suspect.

5. Wire it into CI and pin your build 🔒 

# .github/workflows/ffmpeg-upgrade.yml (sketch)
name: ffmpeg-upgrade-check
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  diff-builds:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./scripts/fetch_ffmpeg.sh old new   # your script; downloads two pinned builds
      - run: python3 upgrade_check.py ./bin/old/ffmpeg ./bin/new/ffmpeg fixtures/sample.mp4 recipes.json

Also record the exact build string (ffmpeg -version | head -1) in your output metadata. When support asks "when did this change?", you can answer in one query.

What's next

  • Read the official 9.0 release notes against your own flags; this post leans on news coverage.
  • Add a min_ssim per recipe if you deliberately want to accept small encoder changes.
  • Pair this with a VMAF check if you already track perceptual quality. Our harness only asks whether the output moved, not whether it got better.

If you run it on a real 8.x to 9.0 diff, I'd love to hear what showed up. #ffmpeg #video #devops

title: Railway Environment Variable Incident: What Laravel & Cloud Application Teams Should Do Now
summary:
On October 21, 2026, Railway disclosed that an unauthorized third party may have accessed the systems that store its customers' environment variables. That exposes a problem that rarely comes up when engineering teams discuss cloud security: what happens when the infrastructure you depend on to recover from an incident is itself affected by that incident?

If your team deploys on a platform like Railway, you have probably already been asked the same question internally: what do we do now?

This post is a practical answer. It's written for Laravel and cloud application teams, and it deliberately avoids alarm. Incidents like this are a reasonable moment to take a breather to check your own setup, and most of what follows is good hygiene you would want in place for your team anyway.

What Exactly Happened?

The facts below come from Railway's own disclosure and from press coverage published on the first day after it. Details are still developing, so treat this as a snapshot:

  • Railway said it detected unusual activity on October 21 in the systems that store customer environment variables.
  • Its initial assessment was that an unauthorized party may have accessed encrypted variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. Reporting describes the affected values as including API keys, database credentials and private registry credentials.
  • Railway paused deployments while it investigated. The Defiant reported that this left customers unable to push updated applications carrying replacement credentials. Enterprise builds were restored late Wednesday, while customers on other plans were still waiting to redeploy.
  • Railway's early analysis suggested the impact may be limited to a subset of users, but it still recommended that every customer rotate every stored secret and review service logs for unusual activity. It has not published a detailed scope.
  • Railway described the incident as part of a series of attacks on platform companies aimed at compromising AI inference providers, and said it had notified upstream providers so they could proactively revoke potentially exposed keys.

One claim is still being examined as this blog was written. A developer has alleged that roughly $370,000 was stolen through secrets stored on Railway. On-chain analysts have tracked funds moving from a suspected attacker's wallet, but the link between that wallet and the Railway incident has not been confirmed.

Why Environment-Variable Exposure Matters?

Environment variables are the standard way to keep configuration out of code. In practice, they're also where applications keep the keys to everything else: database passwords, payment and email credentials, cloud storage keys, signing secrets and third-party API tokens.

That makes them an unusually high-value target. An attacker who reads a single set of variables doesn't need to find a vulnerability in your application. They already hold credentials that your application is trusted to use, and those credentials often work from anywhere on the internet.

Secrets Are Becoming the New Security Perimeter

There is also a structural point here, and it's the main lesson we'd draw from this incident. Secrets are the new perimeter. Attackers increasingly go after the layer that stores and manages credentials, rather than the services those credentials unlock. It's often the softer target, and it can be just as valuable if the stolen keys grant access to paid AI accounts, databases or cloud resources. Your application can be well-written and fully patched, and its security still depends on every platform that holds a copy of its secrets.

The practical conclusion is not "stop using managed platforms." They are vital in removing a great deal of operational burden for growing teams, and most teams are safer for using them. The lesson here is to design in a manner that a single vendor's bad day is survivable, because the credentials it holds are scoped, short-lived and quick to replace.

What Credentials To Review And Rotate Post the Railway Security Incident?

Railway's guidance was to rotate everything stored as an environment variable, and that's the right default for anyone affected. The harder part is knowing what "everything" includes. For a typical Laravel application, work through this list:

  • Application key (APP_KEY). This encrypts sessions, cookies and any data you encrypt with Laravel's encrypter. Rotating it will invalidate sessions and make previously encrypted data unreadable unless you plan for it. Recent Laravel versions support graceful rotation through APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS, which lets old values keep decrypting while new ones are written.
  • Database and cache credentials. DB_PASSWORD, any read-replica credentials, and REDIS_PASSWORD. Also check whether the database is reachable from the public internet; if it is, a leaked password is directly usable.
  • Cloud and storage keys. AWS, GCP or S3-compatible access keys, plus any service-account files stored as variables. Railway noted that it would handle resets for some platform-managed items, such as storage buckets and GitHub connections, but you should confirm that rather than assume it.
  • Third-party service tokens. Payment gateways (Stripe, Razorpay and similar), email and SMS providers, push and broadcasting services (Pusher, Ably), search and analytics keys.
  • AI and LLM provider keys. OpenAI, Anthropic and similar keys deserve priority. They're easy to monetize, they can run up large bills quickly, and Railway has said AI inference access appears to be the attackers' target.
  • Auth and signing material. OAuth client secrets, Passport or Sanctum-related keys, JWT signing secrets, and webhook signing secrets.
  • Registry and deployment credentials. Private container registry tokens, package registry tokens (for example private Composer repositories), deploy keys and Git provider tokens.
  • Wallet and signing keys. If any private key that can move money was ever stored as a variable, treat it as the most urgent item and move funds to a new key.

A sensible order is: anything that can spend money or move data first, then anything that grants access to customer data, then everything else. After rotating, check the logs of each connected service for activity you don't recognize in the window around the disclosure, and keep the old credentials revoked rather than just replaced.

Secret-Management Best Practices to Consider

title: HLS with fMP4 instead of MPEG-TS: FFmpeg commands, playlist diff, and the hev1 trap
summary:
TL;DR

We'll package one encode two ways with FFmpeg (MPEG-TS and fMP4), diff the playlists, then add an HEVC rung and catch the hev1 vs hvc1 tag problem with a one-line ffprobe check you can drop into CI.

📦 Code: github.com/USER/hls-fmp4 (replace before publishing)

HLS used to mean .ts files. Today the spec requires fragmented MP4 for HEVC, AV1 and several newer audio codecs, so if you plan to add any of them you'll want fMP4 in the pipeline anyway. #ffmpeg #video

Versions used: ffmpeg 6.1.1 with libx264 and libx265, ffprobe, and a Linux shell. Newer FFmpeg should behave the same, but re-check the tag defaults in step 5.

1. 🎥 Make a test clip 

ffmpeg -y -f lavfi -i "testsrc2=size=1280x720:rate=24:duration=60" \
  -f lavfi -i "sine=frequency=440:duration=60" \
  -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -shortest src.mp4

2. 📦 Package as MPEG-TS 

# ts.sh
mkdir -p ts
C="-c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -g 144 -keyint_min 144 -sc_threshold 0 -c:a aac -b:a 128k"
ffmpeg -y -i src.mp4 $C -f hls -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_type mpegts -hls_segment_filename 'ts/seg_%03d.ts' ts/index.m3u8
head -8 ts/index.m3u8

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:3
#EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6
#EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE:0
#EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE:VOD
#EXTINF:6.000000,
seg_000.ts
#EXTINF:6.000000,

💡 Tip: -g 144 -keyint_min 144 -sc_threshold 0 makes segments exactly 6 s at 24 fps. Without it the muxer cuts on the next keyframe, which can be 10 s away.

3. 📦 Package as fMP4

Same encode settings, two changed flags:

# fmp4.sh
mkdir -p fm
C="-c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -g 144 -keyint_min 144 -sc_threshold 0 -c:a aac -b:a 128k"
ffmpeg -y -i src.mp4 $C -f hls -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_type fmp4 -hls_fmp4_init_filename init.mp4 \
  -hls_segment_filename 'fm/seg_%03d.m4s' fm/index.m3u8
head -9 fm/index.m3u8
ls fm

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:7
#EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6
#EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE:0
#EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE:VOD
#EXT-X-MAP:URI="init.mp4"
#EXTINF:6.000000,
seg_000.m4s
#EXTINF:6.000000,
index.m3u8  init.mp4  seg_000.m4s  seg_001.m4s  ...

Two differences to remember:

MPEG-TS fMP4
EXT-X-VERSION 3 7
Init segment none init.mp4 via EXT-X-MAP
Segment extension .ts .m4s

The RFC says each fMP4 segment must have an EXT-X-MAP tag, and EXT-X-MAP needs compatibility version 6 or higher (RFC 8216 3.3 and 4.3.2.5). FFmpeg set version 7 for us.

4. 📏 Compare sizes 

cat ts/*.ts | wc -c
cat fm/init.mp4 fm/*.m4s | wc -c

17086568
16523545

That's about 3 percent smaller for fMP4 on this clip. Don't generalize it: this is a synthetic test pattern, and real catalogues will differ. Run it on your own titles.

⚠️ Note: if you try to ffprobe a lone .m4s file you'll see trun track id unknown, no tfhd was found and error reading header. The media segments aren't playable without init.mp4. Probe the init segment, or concatenate init + segment first.

5. 🪤 Add an HEVC rung and hit the tag trap

Apple's authoring spec says HEVC in HLS must be in fMP4, so we're already in the right container. Now package it the naive way:

# hevc_naive.sh
ffmpeg -y -i src.mp4 -c:v libx265 -g 144 -keyint_min 144 -x265-params scenecut=0 \
  -c:a aac -f hls -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_type fmp4 -hls_fmp4_init_filename init_naive.mp4 \
  -hls_segment_filename 'hn_%03d.m4s' hn.m3u8
ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 \
  -show_entries stream=codec_name,codec_tag_string -of csv=p=0 init_naive.mp4

hevc,hev1

hev1 keeps parameter sets inside the samples. The spec recommends avc1, hvc1 and dvh1 over avc3, hev1 and dvhe (Apple authoring spec 1.10). Add the tag:

# hevc_fixed.sh
ffmpeg -y -i src.mp4 -c:v libx265 -tag:v hvc1 -g 144 -keyint_min 144 \
  -x265-params scenecut=0 -c:a aac -f hls -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_type fmp4 -hls_fmp4_init_filename init.mp4 \
  -hls_segment_filename 'hv_%03d.m4s' hv.m3u8
ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 \
  -show_entries stream=codec_name,codec_tag_string -of csv=p=0 init.mp4

hevc,hvc1

💡 Tip: the stream plays in desktop browsers either way, which is why this slips through. I did not test on Apple hardware here, so treat "may not play" as the risk, and check on a real device before shipping.

6. ✅ A tiny CI check 

# scripts/check_tag.sh
set -euo pipefail
tag=$(ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=codec_tag_string -of csv=p=0 "$1")
case "$tag" in
  avc1|hvc1|dvh1) echo "OK: $tag" ;;
  *) echo "FAIL: codec tag is $tag, expected avc1/hvc1/dvh1"; exit 1 ;;
esac

$ ./scripts/check_tag.sh init_naive.mp4
FAIL: codec tag is hev1, expected avc1/hvc1/dvh1
$ ./scripts/check_tag.sh init.mp4
OK: hvc1

7. 🧭 Master playlist and CODECS

Apple's spec requires CODECS on every EXT-X-STREAM-INF. FFmpeg's -var_stream_map writes it for you:

ffmpeg -y -i src.mp4 -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -c:a aac -f hls \
  -hls_segment_type fmp4 -hls_time 6 -master_pl_name master.m3u8 \
  -var_stream_map "v:0,a:0" -hls_segment_filename 'm_%v_%03d.m4s' m_%v.m3u8
grep STREAM-INF master.m3u8

#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=75900,RESOLUTION=1280x720,CODECS="avc1.64001f,mp4a.40.2"

⚠️ Note: BANDWIDTH=75900 here is clearly too low for a real ladder; I did not set VOD playlist type or bitrates on this quick example. Always set BANDWIDTH from real measured bitrates before shipping.

What's next

  • Wire the tag check into your packaging tests for every rendition.
  • Add -g/-keyint_min alignment across rungs (see the segment audit post if you have it).
  • Read Apple's HLS authoring spec sections on video and playlists once; they're short.

Wrapping up: fMP4 is two flag changes away, and the HEVC tag is the one thing that bites. Which codec are you adding next?
