📦 Code: github.com/USER/hls-fmp4 (replace before publishing)

HLS used to mean .ts files. Today the spec requires fragmented MP4 for HEVC, AV1 and several newer audio codecs, so if you plan to add any of them you'll want fMP4 in the pipeline anyway. #ffmpeg #video

Versions used: ffmpeg 6.1.1 with libx264 and libx265, ffprobe, and a Linux shell. Newer FFmpeg should behave the same, but re-check the tag defaults in step 5.

1. 🎥 Make a test clip 

ffmpeg -y -f lavfi -i "testsrc2=size=1280x720:rate=24:duration=60" \
  -f lavfi -i "sine=frequency=440:duration=60" \
  -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -shortest src.mp4

2. 📦 Package as MPEG-TS 

# ts.sh
mkdir -p ts
C="-c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -g 144 -keyint_min 144 -sc_threshold 0 -c:a aac -b:a 128k"
ffmpeg -y -i src.mp4 $C -f hls -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_type mpegts -hls_segment_filename 'ts/seg_%03d.ts' ts/index.m3u8
head -8 ts/index.m3u8

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:3
#EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6
#EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE:0
#EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE:VOD
#EXTINF:6.000000,
seg_000.ts
#EXTINF:6.000000,

💡 Tip: -g 144 -keyint_min 144 -sc_threshold 0 makes segments exactly 6 s at 24 fps. Without it the muxer cuts on the next keyframe, which can be 10 s away.

3. 📦 Package as fMP4

Same encode settings, two changed flags:

# fmp4.sh
mkdir -p fm
C="-c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -g 144 -keyint_min 144 -sc_threshold 0 -c:a aac -b:a 128k"
ffmpeg -y -i src.mp4 $C -f hls -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_type fmp4 -hls_fmp4_init_filename init.mp4 \
  -hls_segment_filename 'fm/seg_%03d.m4s' fm/index.m3u8
head -9 fm/index.m3u8
ls fm

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:7
#EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6
#EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE:0
#EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE:VOD
#EXT-X-MAP:URI="init.mp4"
#EXTINF:6.000000,
seg_000.m4s
#EXTINF:6.000000,
index.m3u8  init.mp4  seg_000.m4s  seg_001.m4s  ...

Two differences to remember:

MPEG-TS fMP4
EXT-X-VERSION 3 7
Init segment none init.mp4 via EXT-X-MAP
Segment extension .ts .m4s

The RFC says each fMP4 segment must have an EXT-X-MAP tag, and EXT-X-MAP needs compatibility version 6 or higher (RFC 8216 3.3 and 4.3.2.5). FFmpeg set version 7 for us.

4. 📏 Compare sizes 

cat ts/*.ts | wc -c
cat fm/init.mp4 fm/*.m4s | wc -c

17086568
16523545

That's about 3 percent smaller for fMP4 on this clip. Don't generalize it: this is a synthetic test pattern, and real catalogues will differ. Run it on your own titles.

⚠️ Note: if you try to ffprobe a lone .m4s file you'll see trun track id unknown, no tfhd was found and error reading header. The media segments aren't playable without init.mp4. Probe the init segment, or concatenate init + segment first.

5. 🪤 Add an HEVC rung and hit the tag trap

Apple's authoring spec says HEVC in HLS must be in fMP4, so we're already in the right container. Now package it the naive way:

# hevc_naive.sh
ffmpeg -y -i src.mp4 -c:v libx265 -g 144 -keyint_min 144 -x265-params scenecut=0 \
  -c:a aac -f hls -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_type fmp4 -hls_fmp4_init_filename init_naive.mp4 \
  -hls_segment_filename 'hn_%03d.m4s' hn.m3u8
ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 \
  -show_entries stream=codec_name,codec_tag_string -of csv=p=0 init_naive.mp4

hevc,hev1

hev1 keeps parameter sets inside the samples. The spec recommends avc1, hvc1 and dvh1 over avc3, hev1 and dvhe (Apple authoring spec 1.10). Add the tag:

# hevc_fixed.sh
ffmpeg -y -i src.mp4 -c:v libx265 -tag:v hvc1 -g 144 -keyint_min 144 \
  -x265-params scenecut=0 -c:a aac -f hls -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_type fmp4 -hls_fmp4_init_filename init.mp4 \
  -hls_segment_filename 'hv_%03d.m4s' hv.m3u8
ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 \
  -show_entries stream=codec_name,codec_tag_string -of csv=p=0 init.mp4

hevc,hvc1

💡 Tip: the stream plays in desktop browsers either way, which is why this slips through. I did not test on Apple hardware here, so treat "may not play" as the risk, and check on a real device before shipping.

6. ✅ A tiny CI check 

# scripts/check_tag.sh
set -euo pipefail
tag=$(ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=codec_tag_string -of csv=p=0 "$1")
case "$tag" in
  avc1|hvc1|dvh1) echo "OK: $tag" ;;
  *) echo "FAIL: codec tag is $tag, expected avc1/hvc1/dvh1"; exit 1 ;;
esac

$ ./scripts/check_tag.sh init_naive.mp4
FAIL: codec tag is hev1, expected avc1/hvc1/dvh1
$ ./scripts/check_tag.sh init.mp4
OK: hvc1

7. 🧭 Master playlist and CODECS

Apple's spec requires CODECS on every EXT-X-STREAM-INF. FFmpeg's -var_stream_map writes it for you:

ffmpeg -y -i src.mp4 -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -c:a aac -f hls \
  -hls_segment_type fmp4 -hls_time 6 -master_pl_name master.m3u8 \
  -var_stream_map "v:0,a:0" -hls_segment_filename 'm_%v_%03d.m4s' m_%v.m3u8
grep STREAM-INF master.m3u8

#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=75900,RESOLUTION=1280x720,CODECS="avc1.64001f,mp4a.40.2"

⚠️ Note: BANDWIDTH=75900 here is clearly too low for a real ladder; I did not set VOD playlist type or bitrates on this quick example. Always set BANDWIDTH from real measured bitrates before shipping.

What's next

  • Wire the tag check into your packaging tests for every rendition.
  • Add -g/-keyint_min alignment across rungs (see the segment audit post if you have it).
  • Read Apple's HLS authoring spec sections on video and playlists once; they're short.

Wrapping up: fMP4 is two flag changes away, and the HEVC tag is the one thing that bites. Which codec are you adding next?

title: MCP Server Security: Essential Best Practices for Robust Pro
summary:
Running an MCP (Multi-Cloud Platform or similar control plane) server without a strong security posture is like leaving your front door wide open. These systems often manage critical infrastructure, sensitive data, or orchestrate complex workflows across various environments. A single vulnerability can expose your entire operation.

I've seen firsthand how easily misconfigurations or overlooked details can turn into major incidents. The good news is that many common attack vectors can be mitigated with a consistent application of security best practices.

What are the MCP server security best practices?

MCP server security best practices involve a multi-layered approach focusing on identity and access management, network hardening, regular patching, and data protection. Implementing strong authentication, least privilege access, network segmentation, and continuous monitoring are crucial steps to safeguard your critical infrastructure.

Let's break down the key areas you need to focus on.

1. Implement Strong Identity and Access Management (IAM)

This is your first line of defense. Weak authentication or over-privileged accounts are common entry points for attackers. Don't skimp here.

  • Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Mandate MFA for all administrative and privileged accounts. This is non-negotiable. Even if credentials are stolen, MFA prevents unauthorized access.
  • Least Privilege Principle: Grant users and services only the minimum permissions necessary to perform their tasks. Regularly review and revoke unnecessary access. This reduces the blast radius of a compromised account.
  • Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Define clear roles with specific permissions. Avoid granting direct access to resources; instead, assign users to roles. This scales better and is easier to audit.
  • Centralized Identity Provider (IdP): Integrate with an external IdP like Okta, Azure AD, or Google Identity. This centralizes user management, enforces consistent policies, and simplifies onboarding/offboarding. 
# Example: Simplified RBAC policy snippet (conceptual)
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: mcp-read-only-dashboard
  namespace: mcp-system
rules:
- apiGroups: ["mcp.example.com"]
  resources: ["clusters", "deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-only-dashboard-binding
  namespace: mcp-system
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: dashboard-viewer@example.com
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: mcp-read-only-dashboard
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

2. Harden Your Network Perimeter

Your MCP server shouldn't be directly exposed to the internet unless absolutely necessary, and even then, with extreme caution.

  • Firewalls and Security Groups: Restrict inbound and outbound traffic to only what's essential. Close all unused ports. Use stateful firewalls.
  • Network Segmentation: Isolate your MCP server into its own dedicated network segment or VLAN. This limits lateral movement if a different part of your network is compromised.
  • VPN/Bastion Hosts: Access the MCP server's administrative interfaces only through a secure VPN or a hardened bastion host. Never allow direct SSH/RDP from arbitrary IPs.
  • DDoS Protection: Implement measures to protect against Distributed Denial of Service attacks, which can render your MCP server unavailable. 
# Example: iptables rule to allow only SSH from a specific IP range
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j DROP

# For cloud environments, use Security Groups/Network ACLs:
# Inbound: Allow TCP 22 from your_bastion_host_ip
# Inbound: Allow TCP 443 (HTTPS) from your_load_balancer_ip

3. Keep Software Updated and Patched

Unpatched vulnerabilities are low-hanging fruit for attackers. This is a constant battle, but a critical one.

  • Regular Patching: Establish a routine for applying security patches to the operating system, MCP software, and all dependencies. Automate this where possible, but always test thoroughly.
  • Vulnerability Scanning: Use automated tools to regularly scan your MCP server and its components for known vulnerabilities. Address findings promptly.
  • Dependency Management: If your MCP solution uses third-party libraries, monitor for security advisories and update dependencies regularly.

4. Secure Data at Rest and in Transit

Data handled by your MCP server, whether configuration, logs, or application data, needs protection.

  • Encryption at Rest: Ensure all persistent storage (databases, file systems) holding sensitive data is encrypted. Most cloud providers offer this as a default or easy-to-enable option.
  • Encryption in Transit (TLS/SSL): All communication with and between MCP components should use TLS/SSL with strong ciphers. Enforce HTTPS for all web interfaces.
  • Data Backup and Recovery: Implement a robust backup strategy. Encrypt backups and store them securely, ideally off-site. Regularly test your recovery process.

5. Implement Robust Logging and Monitoring

You can't secure what you can't see. Comprehensive logging and proactive monitoring are essential for detecting and responding to incidents.

  • Centralized Logging: Aggregate logs from your MCP server, operating system, and all relevant components into a centralized logging solution (e.g., ELK Stack, Splunk, Datadog). This makes analysis much easier.
  • Security Information and Event Management (SIEM): Integrate your logs with a SIEM system to correlate events, detect anomalies, and trigger alerts for suspicious activities.
  • Alerting: Configure alerts for critical security events: failed login attempts, unauthorized access, unusual API calls, system reboots, and resource exhaustion.
  • Regular Audits: Periodically review logs for suspicious patterns. Conduct security audits of your MCP configuration and access policies.

6. Secure Your Configuration and Secrets

Mismanaged configurations and hardcoded secrets are a constant source of vulnerabilities.

  • Configuration Management: Use tools like Ansible, Terraform, or Puppet to manage your MCP server's configuration. This ensures consistency and allows for version control and auditing.
  • Secrets Management: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or certificates. Use a dedicated secrets management solution (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Kubernetes Secrets with external integration) to store and retrieve sensitive information securely.
  • Regular Audits: Periodically audit your configurations and secrets storage for best practices and potential exposures.

7. Plan for Incident Response and Disaster Recovery

Even with the best defenses, incidents can happen. Being prepared is key.

  • Incident Response Plan: Develop and regularly test a clear incident response plan. Define roles, communication channels, and steps to contain, eradicate, and recover from security incidents.
  • Disaster Recovery Plan: Ensure your MCP server and its data can be restored quickly in case of a major outage or data loss. Test this plan regularly.

The Ongoing Journey of MCP Server Security

Security isn't a one-time setup; it's a continuous process. New threats emerge, and your environment evolves. Regularly review your security posture, stay informed about the latest vulnerabilities, and adapt your practices. By consistently applying these best practices, you can significantly reduce your MCP server's attack surface and protect your critical operations.

Considering a managed MCP solution or need expert guidance on securing your existing setup? Many vendors specialize in offering secure, compliant multi-cloud platforms and can help you navigate these complexities. Evaluating providers based on their security certifications, incident response capabilities, and adherence to these best practices is a smart move for any organization.
